explanations.explanation: Yes, light. The man says, "He has driven me away and made me walk in darkness instead of light." (Lamentations 3:2) Notice he says he's walking in the darkness, friend. I think this is a man who's tired of not being able to see where he's going.

Rest is a good guess, but the verse doesn't say it. The man says he walks in darkness "…instead of light." (Lamentations 3:2) The word he reaches for is light, and the dark is what he's walking in. I think that's a lonely way to walk.

Home makes sense with the words "…driven me away…" but the verse doesn't use it. It says he was made to walk in darkness "…instead of light." (Lamentations 3:2) So the missing word is light. The verse keeps its eyes on the darkness.

That's the one. He says, "He has besieged me and surrounded me with bitterness and hardship." (Lamentations 3:5) A siege means being closed in on every side, and he says bitterness and hardship are on all of them. I think that's a heavy way to be hemmed in.

Fire and smoke fit a siege picture, but the man never names them. What he says surrounds him is "…bitterness and hardship." (Lamentations 3:5) Those are the two things on every side of him. I think he's describing how it feels on the inside as much as what's outside.

Thorns and briers sound painful enough, but they aren't in this verse. The man says God has besieged him and "…surrounded me with bitterness and hardship." (Lamentations 3:5) So it's bitterness and hardship, with no thorns anywhere in the verse. Those two words are doing all the work.

The text says the opposite, friend. The man says, "He has walled me in so I cannot escape; He has weighed me down with chains." (Lamentations 3:7) He's walled in and weighed down, so slipping out isn't on the table. I think that's a heavy spot to be in.

False is right. The man says, "He has walled me in so I cannot escape; He has weighed me down with chains." (Lamentations 3:7) He says he cannot escape, so he's not slipping out whenever he likes. Walled in and weighed down with chains, and I think that's a heavy spot to be in.

That's what he says. "Even when I cry out and plead for help, He shuts out my prayer." (Lamentations 3:8) He cries out and pleads for help, and he says his prayer is shut out. I think that tells you how much he needs help. It's a heavy line to read.

The verse doesn't say his voice gives out. It says, "Even when I cry out and plead for help, He shuts out my prayer." (Lamentations 3:8) The problem he names is that his prayer is shut out. That's the part that stings.

No wind in this verse, friend. The man says, "Even when I cry out and plead for help, He shuts out my prayer." (Lamentations 3:8) The one doing the shutting out is God, as he tells it. I think that makes it a much heavier line than a breeze would.

Crooked is it. He says, "He has barred my ways with cut stones; He has made my paths crooked." (Lamentations 3:9) Stones in the way, and the paths bent on top of that. Not even a map app could sort that out.

Steep would be a climb, but that's not what the verse says. The man says, "He has barred my ways with cut stones; He has made my paths crooked." (Lamentations 3:9) His ways are blocked by stones, and his paths are crooked. Nobody says anything about hills.

Mud would slow you down, but the verse never mentions it. It says, "He has barred my ways with cut stones; He has made my paths crooked." (Lamentations 3:9) So the paths are crooked, and cut stones bar the ways. Straight roads are exactly what this man says he doesn't have.

Right. The man says, "He is a bear lying in wait, a lion hiding in ambush." (Lamentations 3:10) Both animals are waiting and hiding, and that's the picture he chooses. I think it shows how it feels to him, like danger could jump out at any moment. It's a scary thing to say.

That's a different picture. The verse says, "He is a bear lying in wait, a lion hiding in ambush." (Lamentations 3:10) The bear and the lion are waiting and hiding, and there's no mention of young anywhere. I think he's picking animals that surprise you.

A sleeping animal isn't the picture here. The man says, "He is a bear lying in wait, a lion hiding in ambush." (Lamentations 3:10) Those two are waiting and hiding in ambush, and there's no den or sleeping in the verse. I think that's what makes the picture so frightening.

Target is the word. He says, "He bent His bow and set me as the target for His arrow." (Lamentations 3:12) A target is the thing everything's aimed at. I think that's about as exposed as a person can feel.

A shield stands in front of arrows, and that's not the man's picture. He says, "He bent His bow and set me as the target for His arrow." (Lamentations 3:12) He's the target, so the arrow is aimed at him. I think it's the opposite of feeling covered.

Guide is a gentle word, but this verse isn't gentle. The man says, "He bent His bow and set me as the target for His arrow." (Lamentations 3:12) So he's the target, not a guide. I think it's a hard thing to say out loud.
True. He says, "He pierced my kidneys with His arrows." (Lamentations 3:13) It comes right after the bow and the target in verse 12. I think this one hurts, friend, and it's okay to say so.

This one is actually in the text, friend. The man says, "He pierced my kidneys with His arrows." (Lamentations 3:13) After the bow and the target in verse 12, the arrows land here. I think this is a painful line to read.

The text says the opposite. The man says, "My soul has been deprived of peace; I have forgotten what prosperity is." (Lamentations 3:17) He has forgotten what it is, so he doesn't remember it. I think the good days feel very far away to him.

False is right. The man says, "My soul has been deprived of peace; I have forgotten what prosperity is." (Lamentations 3:17) Peace is gone, and so is his memory of prosperity. I think that's a lonely place to be.

Hope. The man says, "My strength has perished, along with my hope from the LORD." (Lamentations 3:18) His strength is gone, and he says his hope from the LORD is gone along with it. I think this is the lowest thing he says so far. It's a heavy line, and it's okay to feel that.

A name matters, but that's not what he says perished. He says, "My strength has perished, along with my hope from the LORD." (Lamentations 3:18) So the missing word is hope. I think it hits harder because it's tied to the LORD.

Land isn't in this verse. The man says, "My strength has perished, along with my hope from the LORD." (Lamentations 3:18) His strength and his hope are the two things he says are gone. I think losing both at once would feel like running on empty.

explanations.answer: It remembers and is humbled within him
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. "Surely my soul remembers and is humbled within me." (Lamentations 3:20) After everything he's listed, his soul still remembers and is humbled. I think that's an honest thing to say out loud.

explanations.answer: It has gone numb and feels nothing
explanations.explanation: Numb isn't what he says. He says, "Surely my soul remembers and is humbled within me." (Lamentations 3:20) His soul is remembering, and he says it's humbled. I think that's the opposite of feeling nothing.

explanations.answer: It is angry and wants revenge
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. The man says, "Surely my soul remembers and is humbled within me." (Lamentations 3:20) His soul remembers and is humbled, with no word about revenge. Humbled is a quiet word, friend, and I think it fits.
